facts.text: The basic idea of the camera obscura was known to Aristotle: light through a tiny hole in a wall of a dark room projects an image of the outside onto the opposite wall.
Johannes Kepler gave the device the name camera obscura and used one with lenses to observe the sun around 1604.
Many art historians think some painters of the past used a camera obscura to plan the layout of their paintings.
Before Niépce, around 1800, Josiah Wedgwood laid leaves on paper treated with silver nitrate, but he could not keep the images from disappearing.
Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, a Frenchman (1765–1833), made the oldest surviving photograph taken with a camera obscura; it is dated 1826 or 1827.
The picture, now called View from the Window at Le Gras, shows buildings, a courtyard and trees seen from an upstairs window of his country house in Burgundy.
Niépce coated a polished pewter plate with bitumen, a kind of asphalt that hardens where light falls on it.
Accounts of the exposure time differ: about eight hours, several hours, or even several days in sunlight.
Niépce spent about ten years experimenting before he made the picture.
In 1829 Niépce formed a partnership with Louis Daguerre, who ran the Diorama, a popular show in Paris.
After Niépce died in 1833, Daguerre kept improving the process.
On January 9, 1839, the French Academy of Sciences presented Daguerre's results to the public.
Daguerre first explained in public how to make a daguerreotype in August 1839; he had first hoped to sell the method to subscribers.
Through an arrangement with the French government, which gave pensions to Daguerre and to Niépce's family, the method was made free for everyone to use.
A daguerreotype was made on a silver-coated copper plate made sensitive with iodine; the image was brought out with mercury vapor.
A daguerreotype has a mirror-like surface; it must be held at a certain angle to see the picture.
Each daguerreotype was a single, one-of-a-kind picture; the process made no negative from which copies could be printed.
Early daguerreotypes needed exposures of about 20 minutes, so people being photographed had to sit very still.
Better chemistry and mirror systems that gathered more light soon cut exposure times to under one minute, and neck clamps helped sitters stay still.
By 1850, American photographers were making more than three million daguerreotypes a year.
In 1841 New York City already had 100 photography studios.
By 1860 the daguerreotype had been replaced by paper prints made from glass negatives (the albumen print).
The historian Helmut Gernsheim tracked down Niépce's forgotten plate in 1952; it went to the University of Texas at Austin in 1963.
The plate is now kept in a sealed, oxygen-free case at the Harry Ransom Center.
